Response: We appreciate this helpful suggestion. We conducted a thorough review of the manuscript to ensure consistent use of terms such as “sVariants,” “sGenes,” “effector genes,” and related nomenclature across all sections, figures, and supplementary materials. These terms have now been standardized throughout the revised version.
Reviewer #4:
This manuscript is a complementary study to a recent publication by the same group, which used what appear to be largely the same samples for an eQTL analysis. In the present work, the authors perform a comprehensive splicing QTL (sQTL) analysis on more than 200 samples from knee synovium and cartilage obtained from patients undergoing knee replacement surgery.
From the standpoint of general novelty, there is limited conceptual innovation, as sQTLs have been recognized since 2013 as a major mechanism through which human genetic variants and particularly those identified in GWAS affect gene regulation. That said, the quality of this study is superb. The tools used are standard but well-implemented, the analyses are rigorous, and the overall presentation is of high quality. This paper will be of interest to researchers studying rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory joint disorders, and other autoimmune conditions. The data quality appears excellent, the illustrative examples are compelling, and the lists of significant sQTLs provided in the supplementary tables will be valuable to the community.
We have no major comments, mostly specific comments and clarifications:
1. Comment: It is unclear why the number of samples used in this study (238) differs from the previous eQTL study (243), perhaps explaining the sample retention criteria would help especially if it differed from their previous study.
Response: Thank you for this important feedback, and we apologize for the lack of clarity in the original description of sample numbers. We would like to clarify that the 238 samples refer to all qualified donors included in the present study after quality control, each with matched RNA-seq and genotype data. Among these, 204 donors had high-quality, matched cartilage RNA-seq and genotype data, consistent with the sample size reported in our previous cartilage eQTL study, and 202 donors had high-quality, matched synovium RNA-seq and genotype data. 168 donors have both qualified cartilage and synovium RNA-seq data (as shown in Figure 18a below).
The number 243 refers to the number of donors included in our previous synovium eQTL study after genotype data quality control but prior to RNA-seq data quality control (Figure 18b). Of these, 41 samples were further excluded due to either missing matched synovium RNA-seq data or RNA-seq data failed quality control, and 202 samples were retained for downstream analyses, which corresponds exactly to the synovium samples analyzed in the current study. Therefore, the samples used here are fully consistent with those in our previous studies, and no additional quality control was applied beyond what has already been described.
To minimize potential confusion regarding sample numbers, we have added the Figure 18a below as a new supplementary figure in the revised manuscript and added more detailed sample donor description in Methods section to provide a clear overview of sample information (Main text, Lines 384-389; Supplementary Figure 1a).
Figure 18. Clarification of sample sizes. (a) Venn diagram showing the number of donors with high-quality, matched cartilage and synovium RNA-seq and genotype data included in this study. (b) Overview of donor inclusion and exclusion at each quality control step in the previous synovium eQTL study, indicating the number of donors retained or removed due to missing synovium RNA-seq data or failing RNA-seq or genotype quality control, resulting in 202 donors with matched genotype and synovium RNA-seq data.
2. Comment: Figure 2e has a typo in the x axis label. Please change “sVraint” to “sVariant”.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We apologize for the erroors in the manuscript and any inconvenience caused. All errors have been corrected, and the manuscript has been carefully revised to improve clarity and accuracy. We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading and helpful suggestions.
3. Comment: Figure 3a: Please clarify what the blue and red distributions represent. I assume that red corresponds to sVariants and blue to eVariants, but this should be explicitly stated. They are specified in figure 6.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful comment. We apologize for the missing figure legend and the inconvenience caused. We have added the legend for Figure 3a in the revised version.
4. Comment: SpliceAI threshold: The rationale for using a 0.3 cutoff for SpliceAI is unclear. Was this based on prior benchmarking or empirically determined in this dataset? Further, calling SpliceAI overlap “cross-validation” is misleading, cross validation has a very specific meaning in machine learning.
Response: Thank you for this insightful comment. We apologize for the earlier lack of clarity. In our analysis, we used a SpliceAI cutoff of 0.2, which was selected based on the benchmarking reported in the original SpliceAI publication1. In that study, Jaganathan et al. showed that a threshold of 0.2 achieves a high sensitivity of approximately 80%, although the validation rate at this cutoff is relatively modest (~30%). Because our primary objective was to comprehensively capture potential splice-altering variants, we prioritized high sensitivity to avoid missing functionally relevant candidates. Importantly, the relatively lower validation rate associated with this threshold can be effectively compensated by integrating our sQTL data, which provides orthogonal genetic evidence for splice-altering effects. By leveraging the complementarity between computational predictions (high sensitivity) and statistical association signals (high specificity), this combined strategy enables us to identify as many bona fide functional variants as possible, while reducing false positives that may arise from SpliceAI alone.
We also agree with the reviewer that referring to this overlap as “cross-validation” was inappropriate, as the term has a specific technical meaning in machine learning. We have revised the manuscript accordingly and now describe the integration as a complementary validation strategy rather than cross-validation.
5. Comment: Unannotated splice events: One potential missed opportunity was the identification of de novo or previously unannotated splice junctions arising from genetic variants. Did the analysis pipeline allow for detection of unannotated intron-exon junctions, or was it restricted to reference-annotated events?
Response: Thank you for this valuable comment. Our analysis pipeline does allow for the discovery of previously unannotated splice junctions. Specifically, we used LeafCutter for splicing quantification, which is annotation-independent and identifies splice events directly from the genomic coordinates of junction-spanning reads. As a result, our workflow is capable of detecting de novo or unannotated splice junctions that are not present in existing gene models.
To assess this explicitly, we compared all significant introns identified in cartilage and synovium with the GENCODE v19 annotation. We found that 17% of significant introns in cartilage and 19% in synovium correspond to unannotated splice junctions (Figure 19). These results highlight the ability of our approach to uncover novel splicing events that would be missed by annotation-restricted methods. These results have been added to the revised manuscript (Main text, Lines 98-104; Supplementary Figure 4).
Figure 19. Classification of introns according to whether both intron boundaries, one intron boundary, or neither intron boundary are annotated in GENCODE v19.
6. Comment: Enrichment analysis: Please clarify how enrichment was computed. Was the background a random set of all genes, or a random subset of expressed genes matched for tissue expression level? This distinction is important for interpreting enrichment magnitudes.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. We have clarified the definition of the background sets used in each enrichment analysis. For the tissue-specific sQTL gene enrichment, the background consisted of all genes included in the tissue-specific sQTL analysis, ensuring that both the test set and background were drawn from the same pool of genes tested for tissue specificity.
For the height GWAS-colocalized sQTL gene enrichment, the background set included all cartilage genes that were eligible for the colocalization analysis, thereby matching the background to the set of genes with sufficient expression and genetic signal for colocalization testing.
These clarifications have been added to the Methods section to make the enrichment framework fully transparent and interpretable (Main text, Lines 559-562).
7. Comment: Terminology (“synovium-specific”): Consider avoiding the term synovium-specific for genes detected only in synovium but not in cartilage. For instance, IRF5 was only observed in synovium here, yet it is a well-known transcription factor induced in multiple inflammatory contexts. “Detected only in synovium” or “preferentially expressed in synovium” might be less misleading than “specific.”
Response: Thank you for your helpful suggestions. As suggested, we have revised all expressions like “synovium-specific sGene” to “sGene only detected in synovium” to make them less misleading.
8. Comment: Figure 4i and distal sVariants: I assume that the example shown in Figure 4i is an illustrative case rather than a general trend, and that most distal sVariants were not located within clearly defined or shared DNA-accessible or transcriptionally active regions. Please clarify whether this was generally observed. Which fraction of lead or fine mapped sQTLs reside within accessible regions.
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. We agree that the locus shown in Fig. 4i is intended as an illustrative example; however, the observation that distal sVariants overlap accessible/active regulatory regions is not limited to a few isolated cases. To clarify this point, we performed a systematic epigenomic annotation analysis and added the results as new supplementary materials (Main text, Lines 162-168; Supplementary Figure 12; Supplementary Tables 13,14).
First, using lead sVariants, we observed significant enrichment in open and active chromatin marks, including ATAC-seq peaks and H3K27ac peaks (Fig. 20a), supporting the idea that many lead sQTL variants fall within regulatory regions that are accessible and/or transcriptionally active.
Second, we fine-mapped all sQTL signals and annotated variants in the 95% credible sets. We found that more than two-thirds of sQTL signals had at least one credible-set variant overlapping ATAC-seq and/or H3K27ac peaks (Fig. 20b). Moreover, approximately one-third of sQTL signals had at least one credible-set variant supported by both ATAC-seq and H3K27ac annotations (Fig. 20b). Together, these results indicate that overlap with accessible/active regulatory regions is a general pattern, rather than being driven by a small number of loci.
Finally, to address the reviewer’s point on “distal” sVariants, we examined the distance between annotated sVariants and their target splice sites. We observed that >20% of annotated sVariants are located >50 kb from the target splice site (Fig. 20c), indicating that distal regulatory sVariants are also a frequent feature of our data rather than rare exceptions.
Figure 20. Epigenetic annotation of sVariants. (a) The enrichment of lead sVariants across different epigenetic markers. Dots represent odds ratios, and the whiskers represent 95% CIs. (b) Bar plot showing epigenetic annotation results of fine-mapped sVariants. (c) Histogram showing the distribution of distances between the enhancer marker annotated credible set sVariants and their target splice sites.
9. Comment: Negative control (“mental disorders”): Is “mental disorders” an appropriate negative control category, given the vastly different expression profiles between synovium/cartilage and brain? If the goal was to include a trait set with minimal overlap in expression context.
Response: Thank you for raising this point. We would like to clarify that stratified LD score regression (S-LDSC) is used to identify functional genomic regions in which GWAS heritability is enriched, by testing whether disease heritability is preferentially associated with specific molecular annotations. When S-LDSC is applied across tissue- or cell-type–specific regulatory features, the results show that disease heritability tends to be enriched in functional elements derived from established disease-relevant tissues or cell types, while little or no enrichment is observed in tissue-specific regulatory annotations from etiologically unrelated tissues2-8. Notably, multiple studies have consistently reported that the heritability of mental disorders is predominantly enriched in molecular features derived from neural or brain-related cell types, with minimal enrichment in non-neural tissues2,5,8.
Based on this rationale, we selected mental disorders as a negative control under the assumption that cartilage and synovium are not causally involved in the pathogenesis of mental disorders, rather than on differences in gene expression profiles between joint tissues and brain, similar to the negative control selection strategy by other studies5,7. Thus, we would not expect the heritability of psychiatric traits to be enriched in cartilage- or synovium-derived eQTL or sQTL annotations, making mental disorder GWAS an appropriate biological negative control in this context.
10. Comment: Power and saturation: Do the authors have an estimate of how far from saturation the current sQTL discovery is? In other words, how many additional samples would be needed to approach saturation in sQTL detection for these tissues? Such estimates would help contextualize the study’s power.
Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have performed a formal power analysis to assess the current degree of sQTL discovery saturation and to estimate the sample sizes required to detect additional signals.
Based on this analysis, with our current sample size (~200 donors), the statistical power is already close to 1.0 for variants with MAF > 0.15, and approximately 0.8 for variants with MAF around 0.10. In contrast, power is substantially lower for variants with MAF < 0.05, indicating that sQTL discovery for low-frequency variants is not yet saturated. The analysis further shows that increasing the sample size to ~400 donors would raise power for MAF around 0.05 variants to approximately 0.8, whereas detecting sQTLs driven by rarer variants (MAF < 0.01) would require >1,000 samples to achieve comparable power.
Figure 21. Power analysis of cis-sQTL showing statistical power to detect cis-sQTL across different MAF and sample sizes. We assume α = 0.05/2,500,000, reflecting Bonferroni correction for 2,500,000 hypotheses based on 50,000 intron clusters and an average of 50 non-redundant SNPs in the region ±1 Mb of each intron cluster.
These results indicate that our current dataset is well powered for common sQTLs, but that additional samples would primarily increase discovery for low-frequency and rare variants, rather than substantially altering conclusions for common variants. We have added these power estimates to the revised manuscript to better contextualize the study’s power and to provide guidance for future sQTL studies in synovium and cartilage (Main text, Lines 94-96; Supplementary Figure 3).
11. Comment: Data reuse and new datasets: The HRA004624 dataset was already used in the authors’ previous eQTL study (Nat. Commun., 2024; [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-45652-x]*). However, dataset HRA006224 was not available from GSA at the time of review, making it unclear whether it constitutes new data. The authors should clarify whether this study includes any non-overlapping samples relative to the prior eQTL analysis and what is the HRA006224 contributing to this study since it seems that all data was already available from the previous study.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We confirm that the current study uses exactly the same set of samples as our previous eQTL publication, and no additional or non-overlapping samples were included. The dataset HRA006224 corresponds to the same sequencing data and was generated as part of the same cohort; it has now been released and is publicly accessible through the GSA repository at the time of revision (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/browse/HRA006224). We have clarified this in the revised manuscript to avoid any misunderstanding regarding data reuse and availability.
12. Comment: While new methods may not have been developed. We still think the methods reported lack in detail, for example the exact pipeline ran (with software versions and parameters) would help readers be able to replicate their study.
Response: Thank you for this helpful comment. We agree that providing sufficient methodological detail is essential for reproducibility. In the revised manuscript, In the revised manuscript, we have substantially expanded the Methods section to include a clearer and more comprehensive description of the analysis pipeline, including the software tools used, their versions, key parameters, and data-processing steps. These additions ensure that readers can accurately replicate our workflow and analytical results.

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Response: We thank the co-reviewer for their time and thoughtful evaluation of our manuscript. We appreciate the constructive comments and suggestions provided, which have helped us improve the clarity and quality of the work.

Response to reviewers’ comments:
Reviewer #1:
We have reviewed the revised manuscript and response to our comments, and are impressed with the authors' thorough and thoughtful responses to all reviewer comments. We are impressed with the revisions and clarifications provided and have no further questions or requests.
1. Comment: We recommend (if possible, not required) that the authors inquire whether the results from this study could be made available through the GTEx portal.
Response: We sincerely thank the Reviewer for the positive evaluation of our revised manuscript and for the helpful suggestion regarding data sharing.
We have inquired about the possibility of depositing our results in the GTEx portal; however, the GTEx portal does not accept externally generated datasets. Reviewer #4:
The authors have addressed most of my initial minor comments and in response to reviewer’s 1 points have improved their presentation of their analysis. I have 2 small, suggestions
2. Comment: Although the authors do not explicitly quantify the number of sGenes harboring multiple independent sQTLs, Fig. 2a suggests a markedly higher proportion of multi-sQTL genes in cartilage compared to synovium. A rough estimation from the figure indicates that approximately 25–30% of cartilage sGenes harbor two or more independent sQTLs, versus roughly 10–15% in synovium (an odds ratio of 2!). A simple contingency analysis based on these approximate counts yields a highly significant difference (χ² test, p < 1015), consistent with the similar total number of sQTL signals despite substantially fewer sGenes in cartilage. The authors do not comment on this, is it a result of some technical artefact or do the authors think there is a greater number of genes with a more complex splice regulation in the cartilage?
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this careful observation. We agree that the proportion of genes harboring multiple independent sQTL signals is an important feature of splicing regulation.
Upon explicit quantification at the intron-cluster level, we found that among the 960 significant sQTL intron clusters identified in cartilage, 33 harbored more than one independent sQTL signal (3.4%). In contrast, among the 1,680 significant sQTL intron clusters identified in synovium, 102 harbored multiple independent signals (6.1%). Thus, the proportion of multi-signal intron clusters is approximately 1.8-fold higher in synovium than in cartilage. This pattern is consistent with previous large-scale studies, including GTEx and other recent analyses1,2, which have shown that as the total number of detected sQTL genes increases, the fraction of genes harboring multiple independent sQTL signals also rises. This reflects increased statistical power to resolve secondary signals rather than intrinsic differences in regulatory complexity.
To improve clarity for readers, we have updated Figure 2a such that the left y-axis now represents the proportion of intron clusters harboring multiple independent sQTL signals rather than the absolute counts.
3. Comment: Is the case displayed in figure 2h,i general, meaning that lead sQTL SNPs frequently differ between synovium and cartilage for the same regulatory region suggests that the lead SNP is not, in general, the causal variant but rather a tissue-specific proxy within an LD block. This presents an opportunity to further refine causal inference by leveraging cross-tissue differences. For example, in cases where the synovium lead SNP lies closer to a splice junction while the cartilage lead SNP is more distal (or vice versa), functional proximity could help prioritize the more likely causal variant within the shared LD region. Given the concerns raised by Reviewer 1 regarding the distance of causal sQTL variants from splice sites, such an analysis could help re-estimate the fraction of sQTLs whose likely causal variants lie near splice regions versus more distal regulatory elements. This may either strengthen the conclusion that most causal variants act locally on splicing, or alternatively provide additional evidence that a substantial fraction act through more distal mechanisms.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion. We agree that, for shared sQTL events, tissue-specific lead variants may often represent proxies within the same LD block rather than the true causal variant, and that cross-tissue differences could, in principle, provide additional resolution for causal inference.
To further evaluate this point, we performed a splice event-level assessment across n = 1141 shared significant sQTL events between cartilage and synovium. As shown in Figure 1, the lead sVariant was identical in 26.5% (302/1141) of events, whereas 73.5% (839/1141) showed different lead variants across tissues. Among these discordant lead pairs, 78.3% (657/839) were in strong LD (R² > 0.8), consistent with tissue-specific proxy variants within a shared LD block rather than independent signals. For the strong-LD discordant events, we compared the distance of each tissue’s lead variant to the corresponding target splice site. We observed frequent differences in proximity, with a median absolute distance difference of 13,207 bp; 53.0% (348/657) of events had the synovium lead variant closer to the target splice site, whereas 47.0% (309/657) had the cartilage lead variant closer. These findings indicate that cross-tissue lead discordance is common and may provide additional information within shared LD regions.
However, because proximity to the target splice site alone does not establish causality, we did not further prioritize variants solely based on distance. Instead, we have incorporated additional discussion in the revised manuscript highlighting the potential of cross-tissue fine-mapping approaches to refine causal variant inference in future studies (Main text, Lines 333-335).
Figure 1. Cross-tissue comparison of lead sVariants for shared sQTL events. a, Distribution of linkage disequilibrium (LD R²) between lead sVariants of shared significant splice events identified in cartilage and synovium. Each bar represents the number of shared splice events within a given LD bin. b, Scatter plot showing the genomic distance between the lead sVariant and the target splice site for each shared splice event in cartilage (x-axis) and synovium (y-axis). Distances are shown in kilobases (kb). Each point represents one shared splice event. Blue points indicate events in which the cartilage lead sVariant is closer to the target splice site, whereas red points indicate events in which the synovium lead sVariant is closer. The dashed diagonal line represents equal distance in the two tissues.

2. Tian, C. et al. Single-cell RNA sequencing of peripheral blood links cell-type-specific regulation of splicing to autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. Nature Genetics (2024).

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Cartilage and synovium are essential tissues involved in joint-related diseases and traits, including osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and human height. Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify numerous risk loci for these traits, the molecular mechanisms underlying these associations, particularly those involving alternative splicing, remain poorly understood due to the lack of splicing-related genetic data in relevant tissues. To address this limitation, we generate a splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTL) resource for cartilage and synovium. We identify 2,796 independent cis-sQTLs and six trans-sGenes across the two tissues, including 179 tissue-specific cis-sQTLs. Fine-mapping analysis identifies 116 high-confidence functional sVariants predicted to affect splicing through splice site gain or loss, with approximately half located outside canonical splice site motifs. Integration of sQTL data with GWAS summary statistics reveals 12 osteoarthritis, 6 rheumatoid arthritis, and 183 height effector genes in joint tissues. Notably, seven of the 12 osteoarthritis effector genes show joint tissue-specific colocalization. Together with the finding that tissue-specific sGenes play crucial roles in tissue-related biological processes and diseases, our work highlights the significant impact of tissue-specific alternative splicing regulation on disease etiology and provides a valuable resource for further mechanistic validation.

---

## Introduction

Cartilage and synovium are two essential joint tissues associated with multiple joint-related diseases and traits, including osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and human height. OA is the most prevalent chronic joint disease, affecting over 500 million people worldwide and causing pain, disability, and loss of function1. Articular cartilage, the primary site of degeneration during OA progression, undergoes broad molecular disturbances that significantly drive OA pathogenesis2-4. Meanwhile, the synovium plays a crucial role in OA progression5,6, particularly through the production of inflammatory mediators that exacerbate cartilage damage7. RA, a systemic chronic inflammatory disease, primarily targets the synovium, which serves as the major site of inflammation and plays a critical role in disease progression8,9. Moreover, cartilage function is a main determinant of human height10,11. Thus, elucidating the molecular mechanisms governing cartilage and synovium function is essential for advancing our understanding of joint-related diseases and traits.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous genetic loci associated with joint-related diseases and traits12-14. However, uncovering the functional mechanisms of GWAS hits in relevant tissues remains challenging, as approximately 90% of trait-associated variants lie in non-coding regions15. Using expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data from joint tissues as a powerful tool, we and others have identified effector genes for dozens of GWAS loci associated with OA and RA16-19. Nevertheless, many GWAS loci remain functionally unresolved. A plausible hypothesis is that some of these unresolved loci might act by regulating other molecular processes, such as alternative splicing, which has been implicated in various pathological conditions and complex traits20-23. Therefore, the availability of splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTL) resources for joint tissues would be invaluable for resolving the remaining GWAS loci associated with joint-related diseases and phenotypes, offering further insight into the regulatory roles of genetic variants. However, no sQTL data from cartilage and synovium have been available until now.

In this work, we perform sQTL analyses in both cartilage and synovium tissues using samples from over 200 donors. We identify 2,340 genes with significant sQTLs. By complementary validation between deep learning-based predictions and sQTL effects, we pinpoint more than 100 high-confidence functional variants that influence splicing by inducing splice site gain or loss, including many located outside canonical splice site motifs. Additionally, we identify 179 tissue-specific sQTLs, and functional analyses suggest that tissue-specific sGenes play crucial roles in tissue-relevant biological processes and pathological mechanisms. Furthermore, we observe strong enrichment of joint-related trait heritability in the sQTLs from cartilage and synovium. Through colocalization analyses, we identify additional effector genes for OA, RA, and human height. These findings highlight the importance of integrating sQTL signals to illuminate the roles of genetically regulated alternative splicing in disease etiology and complex traits.

## Results

To investigate the genetic regulation of alternative splicing in cartilage and synovium, we utilized our existing datasets from 238 donors who underwent total knee replacement surgery. These included 204 cartilage and 202 synovium RNA-seq datasets, as well as matched blood genotype data (4,293,131 common variants with MAF > 0.05)18,24 (Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1). We performed cis-sQTL mapping by testing associations between intron usage ratios (measured as PSI (percent spliced in) and calculated using LeafCutter25) and the genotypes of all variants located within ± 1 Mb of each intron cluster, followed by conditional analyses to identify independent signals. At a 5% false discovery rate (FDR), we identified 997 and 1,198 independent cis-sQTLs associated with alternative splicing events of 960 and 1,680 intron clusters in cartilage and synovium, respectively (Figure 2a, Supplementary Figure 2). Power analysis indicated that with our current sample size, the statistical power was already close to 1.0 for variants with MAF > 0.15, and approximately 0.8 for variants with MAF around 0.10 (Supplementary Figure 3).

We next annotated the introns with significant sQTLs using two annotation resources to assess whether they represented novel splicing events or had been previously annotated. First, we evaluated these introns against the GENCODE v19 annotation. Based on this comparison, 83% of significant introns in cartilage and 81% in synovium were fully annotated, with both splice junction boundaries matching GENCODE v19. An additional 11% of introns in cartilage and 13% in synovium had only one boundary annotated, whereas the remaining 6% of introns in both tissues had neither boundary annotated in GENCODE v19 (Supplementary Figure 4a). Second, we annotated the same set of introns using Snaptron26, a large-scale splice-junction database constructed from tens of thousands of public human RNA-seq samples. Using Snaptron, we found that only 11 introns (0.66%) in cartilage and 20 introns (0.64%) in synovium lacked supporting evidence in the database (Supplementary Figure 4b).

We aligned intron clusters with significant cis-sQTLs to 854 and 1,486 genes in cartilage and synovium, respectively (referred to hereafter as sGenes) (Supplementary Data 1,2). Over 97% of these genes were protein-coding (Supplementary Figure 5), and approximately 90% of variants were associated with a single sGene (Supplementary Figure 6). A total of 267 sGenes harbored more than one intron cluster with significant cis-sQTLs (Figure 2b and Supplementary Data 3,4). To assess the independence of regulatory signals within the same gene, we calculated the linkage disequilibrium (LD) R2 between the lead sVariants (the significant sVariants with the smallest P value in each sQTL signal) of different intron clusters. This analysis revealed a broad “U-shaped” distribution. Specifically, for 38.0% and 36.8% of these genes in cartilage and synovium, respectively, the lead-sVariant pairs showed LD R2 > 0.5, suggesting a potential coregulation model of different intron clusters for these genes (Supplementary Figure 7). In contrast, more than 60% of all lead-sVariant pairs showed LD R2 < 0.5 (Figure 2c), indicating a high proportion of independent genetic effects on alternative splicing of distinct intron clusters within the same gene. As an illustrative example of independent regulation, in synovium, rs2269219 and rs536765 were found to regulate the alternative splicing of intron cluster 1 and intron cluster 2 of the FECH gene, respectively (Figure 2d). The dosage of the C allele at rs536765 was associated with reduced usage of intron junction 3 (chr18:55222184-55230106) in intron cluster 2 (Figure 2d), leading to retention of exon 7 in the final transcript. Meanwhile, the A allele at rs2269219 was correlated with increased usage of intron junction 1 (chr18:55238835-55240478) in intron cluster 1, thereby promoting inclusion of the longer exon 4 in the final transcript (Figure 2d). These two variants were largely independent (LD R2 = 0.06). Consistent with these effects, individuals homozygous for C/C at rs536765 and A/A at rs2269219 showed the highest expression proportion of the isoform ENST00000585494, which contains both exon 7 and the longer exon 4 (Figure 2e). This finding illustrates how independent variants can act in combination on separate intron clusters to influence final transcript isoforms in a combinatorial manner. Additionally, we examined trans-effects on alternative splicing and identified six significant trans-sGenes across the two tissues (Supplementary Figure 8 and Supplementary Data 5). A larger sample size will be necessary to increase statistical power and identify additional trans-sGenes.

We next compared cis-sQTLs with cis-eQTLs from our previous analyses18,19. In cartilage and synovium, 60.3% and 53.2% of sGenes did not overlap with eGenes identified from cis-eQTL mapping, respectively (Figure 2f). Even among genes identified as both sGenes and eGenes, about 50% of sQTL-eQTL lead-sVariant pairs had LD R2 < 0.5 (Figure 2g), indicating largely independent genetic mechanisms underlying alternative splicing and gene-level expression. Colocalization analysis further confirmed that approximately 62% of sGenes in cartilage and 61% in synovium were either uniquely regulated by sQTLs or influenced by sQTL signals distinct from eQTLs (Supplementary Figure 9). Only about 25% of sGenes shared the same causal variant for both alternative splicing and gene expression. For example, rs149871778 was the lead variant for both the sQTL and eQTL affecting M6PR in both tissues, with a high posterior probability of sharing the same causal variant (PP4 ≈ 1) (Supplementary Figure 10). In contrast, H6PD exhibited both sQTL and eQTL signals, but these were driven by distinct causal variants in cartilage and synovium (LD R2 between lead variants < 0.1; Figure 2h). CPNE3, meanwhile, was regulated exclusively at the splicing level, showing no significant eQTL signals (Figure 2i). These results reinforce that splicing and gene-level expression can be regulated independently, underscoring the importance of investigating splicing QTLs to gain a more complete understanding of regulatory variation in joint tissues.

We next examined the genomic distance between lead sVariants and their target splice site. Approximately 75% of lead sVariants were located within 50 kb of the associated splice site, and more than 90% were within 200 kb (Supplementary Figure 11). Compared with eQTLs, we found lead sVariants were significantly closer to their associated splice sites than lead eVariants were to transcription start sites (TSS) (P < 2 × 10-16, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 2j), suggesting that genetic regulation of alternative splicing is, on average, more proximal than that of gene expression.

Epigenomic annotation and enrichment analyses further revealed that lead sVariants, similar to lead eVariants, were significantly enriched in open chromatin regions marked with ATAC-seq peaks and active histone modifications, including H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and H3K36me3, while being depleted in repressive chromatin marks (H3K27me3 and H3K9me3) (Supplementary Figure 12). These results indicate that although alternative splicing and gene expression often involve distinct causal variants and regulatory architectures, they tend to localize to shared classes of active regulatory elements, reflecting partially overlapping chromatin contexts.

We conducted enrichment analysis of sVariants to characterize their genomic distribution based on SnpEff annotation27. Unlike eQTLs, sQTLs showed the strongest enrichment in splice donor and acceptor regions (Figure 3a), indicating that the perturbation of splice site sequences is a key regulatory mechanism for alternative splicing. To systematically identify functional sVariants and their effects on splice site gain or loss, we employed SpliceAI28, a deep learning- based model that predicts splice-altering consequences of genetic variants using a sequence-only approach and reports confidence scores (Δ scores) ranging from 0 to 1. SpliceAI predictions with Δ score ≥ 0.2 were compared with our sQTL results to validate both the genomic location and regulatory direction of the predicted splicing effects (Figure 3b and Supplementary Figure 13). Using this approach, we identified 116 functional sVariants that regulate alternative splicing by influencing splice site usage in cartilage and synovium (Figure 3b and Supplementary Data 6).

These functional sVariants were predominantly located near their target splice sites, implying direct disruption or creation of canonical splice site motifs (splice donor: 5’-G|GT-3’, splice acceptor: 5’-AG|-3’) (Figure 3c). For example, SpliceAI predicted that the G-to-A transition at rs7724759 disrupts the adjacent splice donor site (Δ score = 0.32). Consistent with this, our sQTL results from cartilage and synovium samples showed that this transition led to skipping of the exon, with its 3’ end defined by rs7724759 (Figure 3d and Supplementary Figure 14a). Among these nearby functional sVariants, we identified 15 and 22 sVariants that directly perturb the canonical GT sequence at splice donor sites or AG sequence at splice acceptor sites in cartilage and synovium, respectively (Supplementary Data 6). As expected, these sVariants exhibited clear genotype-dependent effects on splice-site usage, in which heterozygous individuals typically exhibited a substantial reduction in splicing, whereas individuals homozygous for the motif-disrupting allele exhibited almost complete loss of splicing at the affected site (Supplementary Figure 15).

Notably, 57 (49.1%) of the identified functional sVariants were located four base pairs (bp) away from their target splice sites, beyond the location of the canonical splice site motif, indicating the involvement of additional regulatory mechanisms (Figure 3c). One such example is rs4072037. SpliceAI predicted that it affects MUC1 splicing with high confidence (Δ score = 0.68), where the G-to-A transition leads to the loss of the splice acceptor site 34 bp upstream and the gain of another site 7 bp upstream, without disrupting the canonical splice site motif. This prediction was supported by our sQTL data from synovium and cartilage samples (Figure 3e and Supplementary Figure 14b).

To investigate the tissue specificity of sQTLs, we compared our results with data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx)29 project using mash30 analysis. Consistent with previous studies20,29, we observed low tissue specificity by sign and significantly higher tissue specificity by effect size (magnitude) (Supplementary Figure 16). To provide a quantitative assessment of tissue specificity, we calculated a tissue specificity score as described previously31. The tissue-specificity scores for cartilage and synovium sQTLs were 0.27 and 0.26, respectively.

Focusing on our two joint tissues, we identified 51 cartilage-specific and 128 synovium-specific sQTL-sGene pairs (Figure 4a and Supplementary Data 7,8), respectively. Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that synovium-specific sGenes were significantly overrepresented in immune-related pathways (Figure 4b), consistent with the inflammatory processes known to occur in synovium during RA and OA32-35. Disease Ontology (DO) analysis further highlighted strong enrichment of these genes in immune disorders (Figure 4c). For example, IRF5, a sGene only detected in synovium encoding an interferon regulatory factor, plays a central role in synovial inflammation in both RA and OA33,36 (Figure 4d). For cartilage, although we did not detect significant pathway enrichment, we identified several cartilage-specific sGenes, such as ACAN37 and FOXO138, that are known to be involved in chondrocyte homeostasis and matrix formation (Figure 4e-f). These findings suggest that tissue-specific alternative splicing regulation plays a crucial role in tissue biology and may represent a potential mechanism underlying tissue-related diseases.

Additionally, we observed that synovium-specific sGenes tended to have higher pLI (Loss-of-function Intolerance probability) scores compared to shared sGenes (Figure 4g). A similar but statistically non-significant trend was observed for cartilage-specific sGenes, suggesting that tissue-specific sGenes may be subject to stronger purifying selection. Moreover, tissue-specific sQTL lead variants were located farther from their target splice sites than shared sQTLs (Figure 4h), potentially reflecting the involvement of tissue-specific distal regulatory elements in alternative splicing regulation, such as enhancers39,40. For instance, rs34816914 significantly regulated PAMR1 splicing in cartilage but not in synovium, and was located in a cartilage-specific enhancer marked by H3K27ac and ATAC-seq signals (Figure 4i).

OA is the most common chronic joint disorder. While GWAS have identified over 100 OA risk loci, the contribution of these loci to alternative splicing has remained unclear. By integrating our sQTL data with the OA GWAS dataset12 (Supplementary Data 9), we found significant heritability enrichment41 for multiple OA phenotypes in sQTLs from both cartilage and synovium (Figure 5a). Notably, the enrichment was stronger in sQTLs than in eQTLs, suggesting that alternative splicing plays a distinct and important role in OA pathogenesis. As negative controls, we evaluated heritability enrichment of several mental disorders in the same sQTL datasets, and as expected, observed no significant enrichment (Figure 5a).

To identify specific effector sGenes of GWAS loci, we performed colocalization analysis between our sQTL data and OA GWAS summary statistics. We identified a total of 12 effector genes across cartilage and synovium with high posterior probability of colocalization (PP4 ≥ 0.8) (Figure 5b, Supplementary Figures 17-28, and Supplementary Data 10). Notably, by further integrating sQTL data from non-joint tissues in the GTEx project, our sQTL data aided in identifying seven additional effector sGenes linked to OA risk loci, which could not be identified by sQTL data from any GTEx tissue. In addition, we found that nine effector sGenes were identified either in a cartilage-specific or synovium-specific manner, indicating potential tissue-dependent effects of the corresponding GWAS loci. Finally, for four effector sGenes, their eQTL signals showed no evidence of colocalization with the same GWAS loci in any of our joint-tissues or GTEx tissues (Figure 5c), providing strong support that these risk loci influence OA primarily through regulation of alternative splicing rather than gene-level expression.

COL2A1, which encodes type II collagen, plays a crucial role in cartilage biology42. Colocalization analysis nominated alternative splicing of COL2A1 as an effector event for OA in a cartilage-specific manner. COL2A1 has two annotated transcript isoforms, one containing exon 2 and the other lacking this exon. Previous studies have shown that exon 2-containing transcripts are predominantly expressed in chondroprogenitor cells and early chondroblasts, whereas transcripts lacking exon 2 are the major isoform in differentiated chondrocytes43,44 Our analysis showed that the G allele at rs1793955 was associated with both an increased risk of OA and the retention of exon 2 in the final transcript of COL2A1, but not with the gene-level expression of COL2A1 (Figure 5d-f). This suggests that the higher proportion of the isoform containing exon 2 contributes to OA progression. Further, using paired degenerated and intact cartilage samples from 31 donors (Supplementary Figure 1b), we found a significantly higher usage ratio of exon 2 in degenerated cartilage (Figure 5g). These findings collectively suggest that regulation of exon 2 retention in the final transcript of COL2A1 plays an important role in OA.

Cartilage is an important tissue involved in determination of human height10. By integrating GWAS summary statistics of human height13 with our cartilage sQTL data, we observed significant enrichment of height heritability in cartilage sQTLs (Figure 6a). Colocalization analysis between GWAS and sQTL signals identified 183 effector genes (Supplementary Data 11), of which 79.8% (146/183) could not be nominated using eQTL data (PP4 < 0.5, Supplementary Data 11). These effector genes were significantly enriched in biological processes related to cartilage extracellular matrix organization (Figure 6b), which is essential for cartilage homeostasis45,46 and exerts effects on human height47. For example, we identified PDGFRA (Figure 6c), for which rs6554162 was both a variant associated with human height and the lead variant regulating alternative splicing of PDGFRA without affecting gene-level expression. Previous studies have demonstrated that PDGFRA promotes chondrogenesis48,49. These findings support a role for cartilage alternative splicing in regulating human height and highlight the potential of sQTL analysis to reveal mechanisms underlying complex traits.

In parallel, we observed a significant enrichment of RA heritability in synovium sQTLs. Colocalization analysis identified six effector genes associated with RA risk (Figure 6d, Supplementary Figures 29-34, and Supplementary Data 12). Notably, all of these genes were uniquely nominated using synovium sQTL data rather than synovium eQTL data and four of them could not be nominated using sQTL data from any GTEx tissues (Figure 6d). TRAF1 (tumour necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 1), which encodes a negative regulator of Toll-like receptor signaling in monocytes, has reduced expression associated with increased inflammation and RA risk50. Our colocalization results suggest that alternative splicing of TRAF1 in synovium may contribute to RA susceptibility (Figure 6e). Additionally, FCGR2B, which encodes Fc receptor IIB for IgG, is involved in immune response and has been previously linked to several autoimmune diseases, especially systemic lupus erythematosus51,52. Our analysis indicates that alternative splicing of FCGR2B may contribute to RA susceptibility (Figure 6f).

Taken together, these findings provide a valuable set of candidate genes for future mechanistic exploration of splicing-mediated regulation in OA, RA, and human height, reinforcing the crucial role of alternative splicing in complex diseases and traits.

## Methods

Ethics
This study was conducted in accordance with all relevant regulations regarding the use of human participants and follows the criteria set by the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Xi’an Jiaotong University Honghui Hospital (approval number: 202304005). All patients provided written informed consent before participating in the study.

Dataset and sample information
RNA-seq data of cartilage and synovium, together with genotype data from matched blood samples, were obtained from our previous studies. The raw data are available from Genome Sequence Archive (accession: HRA006224, HRA004624). The dataset comprises a total of 238 donors (163 females and 75 males) (Supplementary Figure 1a,d) who were clinically diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA) and underwent total knee replacement surgery. All donors had matched blood-derived genotype data. Among these, 204 donors had cartilage RNA-seq data. For 173 of the 204 donors, only degenerated cartilage samples were available, whereas for 31 donors, both degenerated and intact cartilage samples were obtained. To ensure tissue-state consistency across all donors, RNA-seq data from degenerated cartilage samples were used for sQTL mapping. The 31 paired degenerated and intact cartilage samples were used for within-donor differential alternative splicing analysis. In addition, 202 donors had synovium RNA-seq data. Donors’ ages ranged from 46 to 84 years, with a median age of 66 years and a standard deviation of 7.44 years (Supplementary Figure 1c). Detailed quality control and data preprocessing procedures were described in our previous publications18,24.

Alternative splicing and transcript-level expression quantification
Clean RNA-seq reads were aligned to the human reference genome hg19 using STAR62 (v2.7.9) based on the GENCODE63 v19 annotation, with parameters set according to the GTEx v8 pipeline. WASP filtering64 was performed during read alignment by integrating genotype data from the same donor of RNA-seq data using the --varVCFfile parameter of STAR to correct for reference mapping bias. Only uniquely mapped reads that passed the WASP filtering were used for downstream analyses. Intron clustering and intron usage ratio quantification were performed using the leafcutter_cluster_regtools.py script from LeafCutter25 (v0.2.9), with intron junctions extracted from BAM files by RegTools65 (v0.5.2; parameters: -s 0 -a 8 -m 50 -M 500000) as input. The leafcutter_cluster_regtools.py script was run with parameters --minclureads 30 --maxintronlen 500000. Normalized intron usage levels were obtained using the prepare_phenotype_table.py script from LeafCutter (v0.2.9) with default settings and used as phenotypes for downstream sQTL mapping. Introns with zero read counts in more than 60% of samples or with insufficient variability (standard deviation < 0.005) were removed. Finally, introns were annotated using GENCODE v19 gene annotations. Intron clusters were retained if at least one intron within the cluster had a splice boundary matching a GENCODE v19-annotated intron, in which case all introns within the cluster were kept. In addition, only intron clusters that could be uniquely assigned to a single protein-coding gene or lincRNA were retained. Transcript-level expression was calculated using RSEM66 (v1.3.1) with BAM files aligned to GENCODE v19 transcriptome as input. The --fragment-length-max parameter was set to 1000, and all other parameters were left at their default values.

cis-sQTL mapping
cis-sQTL mapping was performed using tensorQTL67 (v1.0.10) to test the association between intron usage ratio of each intron that was calculated by LeafCutter and genotypes of variants located within a cis-window of ± 1 Mb upstream and downstream of the corresponding intron cluster. Age, sex, first two genotype principal components (PCs), and PEER factors68 were used as covariates. A range of 1 to 20 PEER factors was tested to maximize the number of significant intron clusters (Supplementary Figure 2). As a result, 11 PEER factors were used for cartilage and 5 for synovium. A grouped permutation procedure (by setting --phenotype_groups parameter for cis mode) was applied for each intron cluster to fit a beta distribution of the strongest association (the smallest P value of all variant-intron pairs tested), and a beta-approximated empirical P values for each intron cluster were obtained. Empirical P values of all intron clusters were subjected to multiple testing correction using the qvalue package69. The intron cluster-level significance threshold was set at FDR < 0.05. Variant-level significance threshold for each significant intron cluster was calculated using the fitted beta-distribution as described in previous studies20,29. Genes with at least one significant intron cluster were defined as sGenes.

To identify independent cis-sQTL signals for each intron cluster, a two-step conditional analysis was performed using cis_independent mode of tensorQTL67, which involved forward stepwise regression followed by backward selection. The lead variant for each independent sQTL signal was reported.

trans-sQTL mapping
Variants with 75-mer mappability scores below 0.9 were first removed. Trans-sQTL mapping was then performed using QTLtools65 (v1.3.1) following the two-step approximate permutation strategy implemented in QTLtools (https://qtltools.github.io/qtltools/). Briefly, a genome-wide null beta distribution of the strongest association P values was constructed based on 50,000 permutations. Empirical P values for each variant-intron pair were subsequently obtained by adjusting the nominal P values using the fitted beta distribution. Variants located at least 5 Mb away from the corresponding intron or on different chromosomes were considered for trans-sQTL analysis. Covariates were identical to those used in cis-sQTL mapping. To further reduce false-positive associations, cross-mapping filtering70 was applied as previously described29. Specifically, genes with mappability scores < 0.8 were excluded, and variants within ±1 Mb of genes that cross-mapped with candidate trans-sGenes were removed. Mappability scores were calculated using k-mer lengths of 75 for exonic regions and 36 for untranslated regions (UTRs). Gene-level P values were then computed to account for multiple introns tested per gene using the formula 1-(1-p))k, where p denotes the empirical P value of the strongest variant-intron association for a given gene and k represents the number of introns tested. Finally, false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied to gene-level P values, and trans-sQTLs with FDR < 0.05 were considered.

Fine-mapping of sQTL signals
Fine-mapping was performed for each significant sQTL signal using the susieR package (v0.14.2) based on sQTL summary statistics. For each sQTL signal, linkage disequilibrium (LD) matrices were calculated using genotype data from the corresponding samples and provided as input to the susie_rss function. We set the maximum number of causal variants to L = 10, fixed the phenotype variance (var_y) to 1, and enabled residual variance estimation (estimate_residual_variance=TRUE), following recommended practice for summary-statistic-based fine-mapping. For each signal, 95% credible sets were derived when available and used for downstream analyses.

Epigenomic data processing
ATAC-seq data from cartilage and synovium tissues were processed using a unified analysis pipeline. For cartilage, ATAC-seq data from 16 cartilage samples derived from osteoarthritis donors were obtained from GEO (GSE108301)71. For synovium, ATAC-seq data from three synovium samples derived from osteoarthritis donors were obtained from our previous study18. Raw ATAC-seq reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) using Bowtie2 (v2.3.5)72. Reads with a mapping quality score below 30 or marked as PCR duplicates were removed. Peak calling was performed using MACS2 (v2.2.7.1)73,74 following previously described procedures75. For each tissue, BAM files from all samples were merged and used to re-call peaks to define a unified peak set. Individual sample peak sets were then compared with the unified peak set, requiring a minimum overlap of 1 bp. Peaks detected in only a single sample were excluded from downstream analyses.

ChIP-seq peak data for six histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3) were collected from publicly available datasets. For cartilage, processed ChIP-seq peak files generated from human mesenchymal stem cell–derived chondrocytes were obtained from the ENCODE project (GEO accession numbers: GSE188124, GSE187652, GSE187044, GSE187055, GSE187641, and GSE187471). For synovium, processed ChIP-seq peak files generated from synovium samples of 11 osteoarthritis donors were obtained from GEO (GSE112655)76. All ChIP-seq datasets were converted to the hg19 genome build using liftOver when necessary. For synovium ChIP-seq data, peaks were filtered to retain only those detected in more than one sample for each histone modification. The resulting peak sets were used for downstream analyses.

sVariants enrichment
All lead variants of independent sQTL signals were LD-pruned with a threshold of LD R2 < 0.8 to generate a query set. For each query variant, 50 random variants were extracted from the SNPsnap dataset77 as a background set, with matching minor allele frequency (MAF), distance to gene, gene density and LD buddy. We annotated both the query and background variant sets using epigenetic data and SnpEff27 (v5.2c), and performed enrichment analysis using the Fisher’s exact test.

SpliceAI prediction and cross-validation with sQTL effects
To investigate whether and which of the significant sVariants exert alternative splicing regulatory effects by mediating splice site gain and loss, we applied SpliceAI28 (v1.3.1) with default settings. SpliceAI is a deep residual neural network that predicts the impact of genetic variants on splice site gain and loss within genes by evaluating sequence context within ±50 bp of the variant position by default. The human hg19 genome sequence, GENCODE v19 gene annotation, and a VCF file containing all significant sVariants were used as inputs. SpliceAI reports predicted splice site gains and/or losses together with corresponding Δ scores for each variant. sVariants with Δ scores ≥ 0.2 that showed concordant effects supported by sQTL data were considered high-confidence functional sVariants.

Tissue-sharing and specificity of sQTLs
Multivariate adaptive shrinkage (mash)30 was applied using the mashr (v0.2.57) package to evaluate the tissue-sharing and specificity of sQTLs. We selected the variant-intron pairs detected in at least 40 tissues (including both our cartilage and synovium tissues, as well as at least 38 other GTEx tissues) and with the smallest P value in each gene as the strong set. The random set was generated by merging the 20 randomly selected variant-intron pairs from each gene. Missing beta value was set to 0, and the missing SE was set to 10. A mash model was then constructed. To estimate the tissue-sharing and specificity of sQTLs between our joint tissues and GTEx tissues, the fitted model was applied to the strong set to get the posterior means and LFSR. To identify tissue-specific sQTLs between cartilage and synovium, we applied the fitted model to all significant independent variant-intron pairs in cartilage and synovium, with the missing beta set to 0, and the missing SE set to 10. Variant-intron pairs with LFSR < 0.05 were considered significant. sQTL-sharing by sign means significant variant-intron pairs have the same direction of mashr-estimated effect size in two tissues. sQTL-sharing by magnitude means mash-estimated effect size is within a factor of 0.5 for significant variant-intron pairs in two tissues.

Joint-related traits associations
We obtained GWAS summary statistics of OA12, RA14 and human height13 from the studies with the largest sample size. The data details were provided in Supplementary Data 9. Additionally, we obtained GWAS summary statistics of multiple mental disorders to serve as the negative controls, including Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)78, Anorexia nervosa (AN)79, Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)80, Major depressive disorder (MDD)81, Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)82, and Tourette syndrome (TS)83. Heritability enrichment of these traits in cartilage and synovium sQTLs was estimated using S-LDSC41 (v1.0.1) according to guidelines (https://github.com/bulik/ldsc/wiki/Partitioned-Heritability). To test the colocalization between GWAS and sQTL signals, we clumped the genome-wide significant variants (P < 5 × 10-8) using PLINK84 (v1.9) with parameters --clump-r2 0.1 --clump-kb 1000 to identify the index SNPs for each GWAS summary dataset. Beta values for all variants located within a ±1 Mb window of the index variant were used for colocalization analysis. For introns within intron clusters with beta-approximated P values less than 0.05 in cartilage or synovium, the beta values for all cis-variants (± 1 Mb) of each intron were extracted for colocalization analysis. For genes showing evidence of colocalization between their sQTL signal and GWAS, the corresponding eQTL signal (beta values for all cis-variants (± 1 Mb) around transcription start site) of the gene were also used for colocalization analysis. Further, to assess whether the colocalized GWAS signals exhibit regulatory effects on gene expression or alternative splicing in other tissues, we integrated sQTL and eQTL signals from 49 GTEx tissues for the corresponding introns and genes identified in cartilage and synovium, and performed additional colocalization analyses.

Colocalization analysis was performed using R package coloc85 (v5.1.0.1) with default settings, which implements a Bayesian test to assess whether two association signals share a consistent causal variant. The analysis reports posterior probabilities for the following five hypotheses: H0 (no association with either trait), H1 (association with trait 1, not with trait 2), H2 (association with trait 2, not with trait 1), H3 (association with both traits via two independent SNPs), H4 (association with both traits via one shared SNP). The results were denoted as PP0, PP1, PP2, PP3, PP4, with higher PP4 indicating greater probability that a single variant affects both traits. After preparation of the input files, we performed colocalization analysis using coloc.abf function with default settings. Genes of which the sQTL signal had PP4 ≥ 0.8 with GWAS signal were considered to be candidate effector genes of GWAS loci.

Differential splicing analysis
For 31 of the 204 donors, RNA-seq data were available for both degenerated and intact cartilage samples, which were used for within-donor differential splicing analysis. For each intron whose sQTL signal colocalized with an OA GWAS signal, differences in percent spliced in (PSI) values between degenerated and intact cartilage were assessed using a paired t-test. PSI values were calculated using LeafCutter (v0.2.9). Introns with a P value < 0.05 were considered differentially spliced, and no fold-change threshold was applied.

GO and DO enrichment analyses
GO and DO enrichment analyses were performed using the R package clusterProfiler86 (v4.16.0) with default settings. GO and DO terms with P value < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. For the tissue-specific sQTL gene enrichment, we used all genes included in the tissue-specific sQTL analysis as background set. For the height GWAS-colocalized sQTL gene enrichment, we used all genes that were eligible for the colocalization analysis as background set.

Data visualization
ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq signals were visualized using Gviz87 (v1.32.0). The Circos plot was generated using circlize88 (v0.4.16). The sashimi plot was generated using trackplot89 (v0.5.7). The gene model was constructed with plotgardener90 (v1.10.2). Other results were visualized using the R package ggplot2 (ref. 91) (v4.2.2).

Data availability
The raw RNA-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive for Human (GSA-Human) at the National Genomics Data Center, China National Center for Bioinformation, under accession codes HRA006224 [https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/browse/HRA006224] and HRA004624 [https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/browse/HRA004624]. These data are available under restricted access due to ethical and legal restrictions regarding identifiable genetic information. Access can be obtained by submitting a data access request to the GSA-Human data access committee, which will review requests in accordance with ethical regulations and participant consent. The expected timeframe for review is approximately 4 weeks. Approved researchers will be required to comply with applicable data protection regulations and data use agreements, and data may be used for research purposes only and may not be redistributed.

The raw genotype data are protected and not publicly available due to data privacy laws. Access to the genotype data can be granted to qualified researchers upon approval by the relevant institutional ethics committee, subject to participant consent and data protection regulations. Requests for genotype data access should be directed to the corresponding author. Whole sQTL summary data have been deposited in the OMIX database (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/omix/) under accession number OMIX015281. The GWAS-sQTL colocalization results and lead variants for cis-sQTL and trans-sQTL analyses are provided in Supplementary Data.

The GWAS data used in this study are provided in Supplementary Data 9. The ATAC-seq data of cartilage used in this study are available in the GEO database under accession code GSE108301 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE108301]. The ATAC-seq data for synovium used in this study are available in the GSA-human database under accession code HRA004624 [https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/browse/HRA004624]. The processed peak files for six histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3) of cartilage are available in the GEO under accession code GSE188124 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE188124], GSE187652 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE187652], GSE187044 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE187044], GSE187055 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE187055], GSE187641 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE187641], and GSE187471 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE187471]. ### Reviewer 1

Key results: In this manuscript, the authors have identified genetic variants that impact alternative splicing of transcripts in cartilage and synovium tissue. They have identified novel sQTLs specific to the synovium and cartilage, and showed that many of the sQTLs colocalize with RA, OA and height GWAS hits, indicating splicing is likely the mechanism of these previously unexplained GWAS hits. The authors also showed that sVariants tended to be tissue-specific and sGenes enriched in trait-relevant pathways.
Validity: The data interpretation and conclusions appear to be generally valid. Answering the questions posed below could help the reader further interpret these results.
Significance: This group reports previously unreported sQTLs for synovium and cartilage, of which some can help explain the mechanism of some GWAS hits. The results further strengthens the evidence that splicing constitutes a significant causal mechanism underlying disease process including genetic risk, in addition to gene expression regulation which historically received more attention from the genetics community.
Data and Methodology: The RNA-seq and genotyping data appear to be of high quality with a large number of samples and good QC methods as described in their previous papers. However, the following questions should be addressed:
• One caveat with the dataset is the genotyping panel does not appear to be very dense, therefore could be lacking the true splice-altering SNPs. It would help if the authors could comment on this and provide a distribution of all the variants detected (regardless of if they affect splicing or expression); what percent of them are intronic, intergenic, exonic, splice site, 5’ UTR, 3’ UTR?
• In comparing the potential role of sQTL vs. eQTL as causal mechanism underlying GWAS risk loci, the eQTL dataset used was previously generated also from joint tissues. This limited-scope comparison is not adequate for inferring causal biology as the biology behind any risk locus may very likely arise from other non-joint tissue and cell types. See suggestions below.
• For sQTL mapping, the authors cite using LeafCutter, however the leafcutter manual recommends using FastQTL for mapping before performing the sQTL analysis in LeafCutter. This appears to be the methodology GTEx followed. Is this what the authors did? Could they expand their methodology accordingly?
Suggested improvements:
• Could the authors confirm the clinical phenotypes of the 238 donors? Specifically do they all have OA (it appears so based on the methods in the cited papers), or did some have RA? If there were non-OA comparators, would be very interesting to comment on how disease status impacts splicing, i.e. whether the sGenes overlapping with the GWAS hits were differentially spliced in OA vs non-OA.
• Figure 2d: Could the authors also show an example of the same variant impacting two intron junctions, and explain how this can happen?
• Figure 2j: Could the authors further elaborate on how close most of the sQTLs are to the target? (e.g. are 90% within 1kb? Etc). A zoomed-in plot like Figure 3c (not restricting to the SpliceAI-predicted variants) could help.
o For the variants further away (e.g. >50kb outside of the gene), is there a hypothesis on how those variants could be impacting splicing? Are they in LD with a closer variant that is not imputed which is the functional one?
o How does the distance of sQTLs from synovium and cartilage compare to the sQTLs from different tissues from GTEx? The GTEx dataset has a whole genome sequencing data & dense genotyping panel, therefore perhaps this comparison could inform if the density of the genotyping panel is affecting these results.
o From what can be gathered in the main text and methods, the eQTLs used for comparison with sQTLs for explaining disease biology and genetic risk are from the authors’ previous eQTL analyses in the same tissues. One cannot assume that RA/OA pathogenesis is concentrated in the cartilage/synovium, therefore it is not adequate to restrict the search space to joint tissues (or any tissue) when making statements about sQTL vs. eQTL underlying genetic associations. The authors should consider either repeating/expanding parts of the analysis related to GWAS loci interpretation by including larger, multi-tissue eQTL datasets such as GTEx, and/or discuss the caveats around findings of sQTL vs. eQTL in explaining genetic associations.
• What percentage of eQTLs and sQTLs impacted multiple genes vs just a single gene?
• What percentage of the alternative splicing events were novel vs previously annotated?
• Figure 3A: Please define ‘splice region’. Are there also otherwise ‘exonic’ variants? The confidence that the functional variant is the causal variant is likely highest for the splice acceptor, donor and splice region variants. For the remaining regions, do you suspect the actual functional/causal variant was not genotyped/imputed? Or could it be true biology that intergenic variants are affecting splicing.

They should result in 100% missplicing for homozygotes and 50% for heterozygotes, is this true?

Of those, is the SpliceAI algorithm less-well trained on synovium and cartilage-specific data? Or do you think the lead sQTL is not the functional variant; the actual functional variant is not typed?
• “Only about 27% of sGenes shared the same causal variant for both alternative splicing and gene expression regulation” -> In these examples, what is the suspected mechanism of a variant resulting in missplicing and differential expression? Are the genes differentially expressed due to splicing causing NMD? Or could transcript annotations be biasing the expression levels?
