### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a high-quality and comprehensive analysis of splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTLs) in cartilage and synovium—two key joint tissues implicated in osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and human height. Using RNA-seq and genotype data from 238 donors, the authors identified 4,133 independent cis-sQTLs and three trans-sGenes, including 309 tissue-specific sQTLs. Integration with GWAS data revealed novel effector genes for OA (14 genes), RA (11 genes), and height (276 genes), many of which were not detectable via eQTL analysis. The study also employed SpliceAI to fine-map 207 functional splice-altering variants, highlighting both canonical and distal regulatory mechanisms. These findings provide a valuable resource and offer new insights into the tissue-specific genetic regulation of alternative splicing and its role in complex trait etiology.
Overall, the manuscript is well-conceived, methodologically rigorous, and biologically meaningful. It represents a significant advance in the field of post-transcriptional regulation and joint disease genetics. The integration of sQTLs with GWAS data is particularly impactful, revealing regulatory mechanisms that are not captured by gene expression alone.
Major Strengths
• Novel Resource: First large-scale sQTL map for cartilage and synovium, filling a critical gap in joint tissue genomics.
• Methodological Rigor: Use of advanced computational tools (LeafCutter, tensorQTL, SpliceAI, mash, coloc) and robust statistical frameworks.
• Biological Insight: Identification of tissue-specific splicing events and their links to disease-associated loci provides mechanistic depth.
• Data Integration: Effective combination of sQTL and GWAS data enables discovery of effector genes not captured by eQTL analysis.
Minor Points
• SpliceAI Scope: SpliceAI predictions are limited to variants within annotated genes, potentially missing regulatory variants in intergenic or enhancer regions.
• Trans-sQTL Power: Only three trans-sGenes were identified, likely due to limited sample size. This aspect could be expanded in future studies with larger cohorts.
• Visualization Density: Some figures are dense and could benefit from clearer annotations and legends to improve accessibility for readers.
• Terminology Consistency: Ensure consistent use of terms such as “sVariants,” “sGenes,” and “effector genes” throughout the manuscript.

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript is a complementary study to a recent publication by the same group, which used what appear to be largely the same samples for an eQTL analysis. In the present work, the authors perform a comprehensive splicing QTL (sQTL) analysis on more than 200 samples from knee synovium and cartilage obtained from patients undergoing knee replacement surgery.
From the standpoint of general novelty, there is limited conceptual innovation, as sQTLs have been recognized since 2013 as a major mechanism through which human genetic variants and particularly those identified in GWAS affect gene regulation. That said, the quality of this study is superb. The tools used are standard but well-implemented, the analyses are rigorous, and the overall presentation is of high quality. This paper will be of interest to researchers studying rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory joint disorders, and other autoimmune conditions. The data quality appears excellent, the illustrative examples are compelling, and the lists of significant sQTLs provided in the supplementary tables will be valuable to the community.
We have no majo comments, mostly specific comments and clarifications:
• It is unclear why the number of samples used in this study (238) differs from the previous eQTL study (243), perhaps explaining the sample retention criteria would help especially if it differed from their previous study.
• Figure 2e has a typo in the x axis label. Please change “ sVraint” to “sVariant”.
• Figure 3a: Please clarify what the blue and red distributions represent. I assume that red corresponds to sVariants and blue to eVariants, but this should be explicitly stated.They are specified in figure 6.
• SpliceAI threshold: The rationale for using a 0.3 cutoff for SpliceAI is unclear. Was this based on prior benchmarking or empirically determined in this dataset? Further, calling SpliceAI overlap “cross-validation” is misleading, cross validation has a very specific meaning in machine learning.
• Unannotated splice events: One potential missed opportunity was the identification of de novo or previously unannotated splice junctions arising from genetic variants. Did the analysis pipeline allow for detection of unannotated intron-exon junctions, or was it restricted to reference-annotated events?
• Enrichment analysis: Please clarify how enrichment was computed. Was the background a random set of all genes, or a random subset of expressed genes matched for tissue expression level? This distinction is important for interpreting enrichment magnitudes.
• Terminology (“synovium-specific”): Consider avoiding the term synovium-specific for genes detected only in synovium but not in cartilage. For instance, IRF5 was only observed in synovium here, yet it is a well-known transcription factor induced in multiple inflammatory contexts. “Detected only in synovium” or “preferentially expressed in synovium” might be less misleading than “specific.”
• Figure 4i and distal sVariants: I assume that the example shown in Figure 4i is an illustrative case rather than a general trend, and that most distal sVariants were not located within clearly defined or shared DNA-accessible or transcriptionally active regions. Please clarify whether this was generally observed. Which fraction of lead or fine mapped sQTLs reside within accessible regions.
• Negative control (“mental disorders”): Is “mental disorders” an appropriate negative control category, given the vastly different expression profiles between synovium/cartilage and brain? If the goal was to include a trait set with minimal overlap in expression context.
• Power and saturation: Do the authors have an estimate of how far from saturation the current sQTL discovery is? In other words, how many additional samples would be needed to approach saturation in sQTL detection for these tissues? Such estimates would help contextualize the study’s power.
• Data reuse and new datasets: The HRA004624 dataset was already used in the authors’ previous eQTL study (Nat. Commun., 2024; [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-45652-x]*). However, dataset HRA006224 was not available from GSA at the time of review, making it unclear whether it constitutes new data. The authors should clarify whether this study includes any non-overlapping samples relative to the prior eQTL analysis and what is the HRA006224 contributing to this study since it seems that all data was already available from the previous study.
• While new methods may not have been developed. We still think the methods reported lack in detail, for example the exact pipeline ran (with software versions and parameters) would help readers be able to replicate their study.
